transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~44 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Maya (Nebula Head ML), Jon (Nebula Infra), Ellen (Nebula Product), Rahim (Nebula SRE)

--- Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood presented week-over-week bench numbers. Median latency improved 18% vs CloudPath on the tuned config, throughput sustained at 430 tokens/sec vs incumbent 310 tokens/sec under the same 4xA10 baseline. Discussed batching, quantization, and KV cache warm patterns; agreed to run tail-latency test and a dedicated slot trial.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:11] Maya: Maya Chen here, head of ML at Nebula. Hi.
[00:00:14] Jon: Jon Park, infra lead.
[00:00:17] Ellen: Ellen, product.
[00:00:19] Rahim: Rahim, SRE.
[00:00:21] Samira: Great. From Redwood we have Diego, our SE, and Lena for CSM. Diego will walk through the bench results.
[00:00:30] Diego: Cool. I'll share my screen, uh, give me a sec.
[00:00:45] [screen share noise]
[00:00:50] Diego: Ok, so slides — week three. First up: methodology recap. We replayed Nebula's sample traffic (anonymized) at 1x and 2x load, measured median, p95, p99, and throughput in tokens per second with steady-state 60 minute windows. Baseline for comparison is CloudPath's managed endpoint profile that Nebula sent. Note: the baseline run used their recommended batching and 8-bit quantization settings.
[00:01:20] Maya: Quick clar — CloudPath used their internal cache warming scripts, right?
[00:01:25] Diego: Yeah they did; we attempted to match warm-up but in some earlier runs the KV cache wasn't fully hot which inflated cold p99s. We added a dedicated warm-up for this run.
[00:01:38] Jon: Can you remind us of the hardware?
[00:01:40] Diego: Redwood ran on a 4xA10 dedicated-like configuration in our POC lab — same GPU class as the CloudPath instance they provided notes for. We used our optimized kernels and continuous batching.
[00:01:51] [00:01:52] Ellen: Alright, show the numbers.
[00:01:55] Diego: Sure. OK slide: median latency — CloudPath: 142 ms median; Redwood tuned: 117 ms median, about 18% improvement. p95 — CloudPath 410 ms, Redwood 325 ms. p99 — CloudPath 950 ms, Redwood 720 ms. Throughput sustained: CloudPath 310 tokens/sec, Redwood 430 tokens/sec with the same concurrent request profile.
[00:02:30] Maya: That's promising. Is that with quantization?
[00:02:33] Diego: Yes, both configs used int8 quantization. We also ran a float16 run: floats slightly better median (110 ms) but higher cost. The int8 run is the sweet spot overall for latency/cost.
[00:02:45] Rahim: Wait — how did you handle batching? CloudPath seems to batch aggressively.
[00:02:50] Diego: We used continuous batching with an adaptive deadline of 18ms and a batch cap of 64 for these traffic patterns. CloudPath's public docs indicate their cap was 96 but with higher latency variability. Our adaptive deadline prevents long queuing for short requests.
[00:03:05] Jon: Were these synthetic tokens or real user text? If our real traffic has longer contexts the numbers might change.
[00:03:10] Diego: Good call. We used Nebula's replayed traffic which includes variable context sizes, average seq length about 420 tokens, tail to 1500 in some traces. We trimmed a few PII segments per your note.
[00:03:25] [00:03:27] Ellen: What's the per-token cost delta?
[00:03:30] Diego: On the bench spreadsheet, raw per-token at int8 is about $0.000013 per token on Redwood dedicated-run vs CloudPath quoted $0.000016 — roughly 19% cost savings before accounting for caching. With prefix/KV caching applied to the 45% of requests that reuse history, effective cost per served token drops further.
[00:03:52] Maya: Do you have the caching breakdown?
[00:03:54] Diego: Yep — cache hit rate in this workload is about 45% for KV/prefix reuse. With cache hits the p99 drops dramatically — our p99 with warm cache was 540 ms vs 720 ms without warm priming in the same run.
[00:04:08] Samira: There's a note in the spreadsheet about tail spikes during tokenization bursts — Diego you flagged that?
[00:04:12] Diego: Yeah, in scenarios where many long-convo requests hit the system simultaneously we saw tokenization overheads at the ingress layer. We recommended moving tokenization to a lightweight edge layer or pre-tokenizing at the client as a mitigation.
[00:04:25] Rahim: Pre-tokenization is tricky for us due to client heterogeneity. Could Redwood provide a small docker shim?
[00:04:31] Diego: We can share a tiny pre-tokenization container script, yes. I'll attach it to the bench sheet.
[00:04:36] [00:04:37] Maya: You mentioned p99 improvements but p99.9 is often what our SLAs chase. Do you have 99.9 numbers?
[00:04:43] Diego: We do. For the int8 run: CloudPath p99.9 recorded 2.4 s; Redwood p99.9 at the same load was 1.8 s. That's still a notable improvement but we're not yet in sub-second world for p99.9 on these peaks without a dedicated slot.
[00:05:00] Jon: Dedicated slot meaning reserved GPUs? How much capacity would you need?
[00:05:04] Diego: For Nebula's 95th percentile traffic pattern our estimate is a 6-GPU reserved pool (A10 equivalent) to keep tail under 1.2s. We recommended autoscaling to 8 GPUs for peak windows.
[00:05:16] Ellen: Any more info on how Redwood handles graceful degradation vs the incumbent?
[00:05:20] Diego: We have automatic fallback to smaller model versions and region reroutes. Also we do partial prefix-caching which preserves latency by serving cached KV slices while the heavier parts are computed. CloudPath's public fallback pattern is less prescriptive; in practice we've seen they return to queued requests.
[00:05:36] [00:05:38] Maya: Security questions — are the benchmark runs on customer data encrypted at rest and in transit?
[00:05:43] Samira: Yes — all POC runs use TLS in transit and customer data on our POC lab is encrypted. We can share SOC2 artifacts and KMS integration notes; Lena is on that.
[00:05:53] Lena: I'll drop the security packet in the shared drive after the call.
[00:05:57] Rahim: For the dedicated-slot trial, what's the expected lead time?
[00:06:00] Samira: Typical lead time for a reserved pool is 7-10 business days once we confirm the commitment level. But for POCs we can often provide a short-term reserved trial within 3 business days with limited capacity.
[00:06:12] Jon: Good. Could Redwood run an end-to-end replay at 2x for 24 hours to capture tails?
[00:06:17] Diego: Yes — that's on my list. We'll run a 24h tail test with KV pre-warm, continuous batching, and peak-concurrency knobs. We'll include p95/p99/p99.9 and cost extrapolated.
[00:06:30] Maya: Something I worry about: CloudPath uses different tokenizer for some nosy tokens and that often changes token counts. Did you normalize tokenizers?
[00:06:37] Diego: We used the same tokenizer that Nebula used in production for these runs. The CloudPath numbers they provided were on a slightly different tokenizer; we applied a token alignment correction which is in the bench sheet notes. There may be minor variance but not enough to account for the latency gap.
[00:06:52] Ellen: Any issues with model determinism or output differences? We care about functional parity.
[00:06:57] Diego: We ran unit evals on a set of prompt templates. Intent preservation is comparable; there are edge-case paraphrase differences with heavy quantization but models pass your quality thresholds in the eval set. We'll include a per-prompt diff report.
[00:07:10] [00:07:12] Rahim: What's the rollback story if we see regressions after scale?
[00:07:15] Diego: We support immediate model rollbacks and can route a subset of traffic to fallbacks automatically. There's also canary routing and A/B testing baked into the rollout UI.
[00:07:25] Maya: Ok so from Nebula's perspective the questions are: 1) tail-latency at 99.9 with dedicated slot; 2) cost projection at 95th percentile; 3) operational playbook docs.
[00:07:35] Samira: Yep, agreed. Diego, confirm the timeline?
[00:07:37] Diego: I'll run the 24h tail test and aim to have initial results by Tue 2026-03-17. Samira will send quant profiles and the bench workbook by Thu 2026-03-12. Lena will drop security docs today.
[00:07:50] Ellen: On billing/contract side, can you provide a short-term reserved trial quote?
[00:07:54] Samira: We'll put together a trial quote — 2 week reserved slot estimate and a path to convert to monthly. I'll get that to Jon by Friday.
[00:08:03] Jon: For the replay data I'll anonymize and share by Friday as well.
[00:08:07] Maya: One other ask — can you show an overlay chart of latency vs queue depth? That helped us before.
[00:08:12] Diego: Yup — I'll add a latency vs queue depth overlay in the bench sheet.
[00:08:16] [crosstalk]
[00:08:18] Rahim: Also please include a run with pre-tokenization shim so we can measure ingress savings.
[00:08:22] Diego: Will do.
[00:08:24] Samira: Any blockers from Nebula?
[00:08:26] Maya: Nothing major. We need to verify legal for the trial but that's standard.
[00:08:30] Ellen: Quick note — product wants to see tail-99.9 for the dialogue flows specifically, not just generic prompts. We'll flag that in the replay.
[00:08:39] Diego: Noted.
[00:08:41] [00:08:43] Samira: Alright, recap to close: Redwood action items — share quant profiles and bench spreadsheet (Samira), run 24h tail with KV warm and pre-tokenization run (Diego), deliver trial reserved quote (Samira). Nebula to share replay and SLOs (Jon/Maya). We'll sync next Tuesday at the same time for the chase on the tail run.
[00:09:05] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[00:09:07] Jon: Thanks.
[00:09:09] Ellen: Bye.
[00:09:10] Rahim: Bye.

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcription occasionally merged proper nouns and acronyms; e.g., CloudPath transcribed as "Cloud path" in some places, and A10 was sometimes captured as "A ten". There are small timing approximations.

References & artifacts shared during the call: bench_spreadsheet.csv (link in CRM), security_packet.zip (link to secure drive), pre-tokenize-shim.tar.gz (attachment).

End of transcript.
